entities.name: Babylonian Talmud
entities.label: Text
entities.summary: The Talmud is the central text of Rabbinic Judaism, and second in authority only to the Hebrew Bible, the first five books of which form the Torah. It is a primary source of Jewish law and Jewish theology. It consists of the part of the Oral Torah compiled in the Mishnah and its commentaries, the Gemara. It records the teachings, opinions and disagreements of thousands of rabbis and Torah scholars—collectively referred to as Chazal—on a variety of subjects, including Halakha, Jewish ethics, philosophy, customs, history, and folklore among other topics.

entities.name: Babylonian Talmud (Bavli)
entities.label: Text
entities.summary: The most authoritative text in Rabbinic Judaism after the Torah itself, compiled over three centuries (c. 200–500 CE) in the great academies of Sura and Pumbedita in Sassanid Babylonia. Consisting of the Mishnah text plus extensive Gemara (commentary/discussion), the Bavli runs to approximately 2.5 million words across 37 tractates. Its pages interweave halakha (legal reasoning), aggadah (narrative, parable, theology), biblical exegesis, history, science, and practical wisdom in a uniquely discursive, non-linear format. The Babylonian Talmud became the definitive legal and intellectual authority for worldwide Judaism, studied daily by millions to this day.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Babylonian Talmud's compilation of halakha and aggadah over three centuries shaped the intellectual authority for worldwide Judaism, influencing Jewish law and culture for centuries to come. Its study by millions daily underscores its enduring impact on Jewish identity.
